title: Avicena raises $100M to link AI chips with microLEDs instead of lasers
excerpt: AI ‘needs a new approach to moving data,’ says Avicena’s new CEO Kevin Pope, as the microLED startup raises over $100M in a Series C.
content_html:
Avicena, a Sunnyvale startup that links AI chips with tiny LEDs instead of lasers, has raised more than $100M in Series C funding. It also has a new chief executive. Kevin Pope succeeds Marco Chisari and will lead the company as it brings its first product to market next year.

InterVest led the round, Avicena announced on Tuesday. Other investors include Tiger Global, Cerberus Capital Management, SK hynix Ventures, Samsung Catalyst Fund and AMD Ventures. Prosperity7 Ventures, Mitsubishi Chemical’s Diamond Edge Ventures and Hitachi Ventures also took part. InterVest director John Dongwoo Ha joins Avicena’s board.

“AI infrastructure needs a new approach to moving data between accelerators, memory, and switches,” Pope said.

Light instead of copper

AI systems move ever more data between accelerators, memory and switches. Copper links face limits on reach, density and energy use, Avicena says. Memory bandwidth and capacity also increasingly hold systems back. SK hynix, one of the investors, has said the memory shortage will last until 2030.

Avicena’s LightBundle platform uses dense arrays of microLEDs and silicon photodetectors linked by multicore fibre. Rather than pushing a few channels very fast, it spreads data across many slower ones. That, the company says, cuts the need for data-rate conversion and complex signal processing.

Because it needs no lasers, the platform can sit close to compute and memory chips. Avicena pitches it for links inside and between chip packages, and across accelerator systems. By contrast, Photon Bridge raised $10M last month to build lasers for AI data centres.

From evaluation kits to a product

Avicena began shipping 1Tbps LightBundle evaluation kits in August. In September, it announced a version with connectors for the ECOC 2026 optics conference. It is meant to make assembly, testing and servicing easier.

The money will go on hiring, product development and engineering, Pope said. Two of the chipmakers behind the round see a role for the technology in memory.

“Energy-efficient optical interconnects are becoming increasingly important to next-generation memory architectures,” said SK hynix Ventures’ Rene Do.

SK hynix Ventures said it hopes to work with Avicena on future memory interconnects. Energy and data movement limit the AI build-out, said Samsung Catalyst Fund’s David Goldschmidt. AMD Ventures’ Patrick Rundell said moving data between compute, memory and networking chips is becoming critical.

Earlier this month, Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum, the Nvidia-backed optical component maker, in an all-stock deal.
